title: Detecting Multi-Hop Reasoning Shortcuts That Skip Verification

original_idea.body:
# Detecting Multi-Hop Reasoning Shortcuts That Skip Verification

**Problem:** A success state: 'we can tell when a model reaches an answer via an unverified shortcut rather than genuine intermediate reasoning.' Backcasting from 'shortcut detection', a prerequisite is identifying an activation signature that distinguishes genuine multi-hop computation from shortcut answering.

**Direction:** On Gemma-2-2B, use two-hop prompts. With circuit-tracer or activation patching, identify prompts answered via the intermediate-hop path vs. the shortcut path. Train a simple probe on activations to predict which path was used and validate by patching out the intermediate-hop feature to see if shortcut-answered prompts are unaffected.

**Why it matters:** Shortcutting underlies unfaithful reasoning and confident wrong answers; detecting it internally supports reliable oversight. Open tooling, single GPU, no training.

**Relevant context:** Circuit Tracing on Gemma-2 (transformer-circuits.pub) found both intermediate-hop and shortcut paths in two-hop reasoning. Unfaithful-CoT detection identifies attention heads driving shortcut behavior (Detecting Unfaithful CoT, substack).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Detecting verification-skipping shortcuts supports oversight of unfaithful reasoning but the chain has a gap.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Circuit-tracer/patching to separate hop vs shortcut + probe needs solid ML; intermediate.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open tooling, no training; reasoning-oversight slice labs underweight.

novelty.reasoning: Two-hop shortcut paths documented; activation-signature detector may be partly open.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Shortcut-path detection extends known two-hop circuit findings.
